claims.text: Aberration-corrected TEM can provide atomic-scale structural imaging of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
In situ heating during TEM will reveal high-temperature structural reorganizations in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Observing such reorganizations would experimentally confirm that the transformations are thermodynamically driven.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are uniform and nearly equiatomic.
The initial nanoparticles have a well-defined high-entropy-alloy structure at room temperature.
A controlled, stepwise heating program will be applied during in situ aberration-corrected TEM imaging.
The experiment will use ultra-high vacuum and controlled temperature ramps.
Atomic-scale defects, local phase separation, ordering, or segregation can mediate thermally induced restructuring.
Thermal activation increases atomic diffusion and vibrational energy.
Increased diffusion and vibrational energy induce local atomic rearrangements, phase modifications, and defect nucleation.
The proposed structural changes are driven by an interplay between high-entropy effects and other thermodynamic contributions.
Heating will produce observable phase transformations or segregation events in the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Heating will produce changes in lattice parameters and possibly form defects.
The room-temperature configuration is a uniform high-entropy state that can serve as the experimental baseline.
The hypothesis is limited to nanoparticle sizes and heating rates for which beam-induced effects are minimal and thermal activation is sufficient.
Very small or irregular nanoparticles, or artifact-producing heating conditions, may prevent the expected atomic-scale changes from being observed.
The temperature thresholds and extent of rearrangement required for a measurable phase transition are not known precisely.
Electron-beam effects may complicate attribution of observed structural changes to heating.
Lattice spacing, defect density, phase boundaries, and segregated regions can be measured as functions of temperature.
The hypothesis is falsified if no significant atomic-scale changes occur at theoretically predicted temperatures, or if all apparent changes are attributable to artifacts.
